name: Breakup of Pangaea
summary: The supercontinent split into Laurasia and Gondwana; India drifted north and hit Asia ~50 million years ago.
details: Pangaea, the supercontinent assembled around 335 million years ago, began to rift about 200 million years ago as magma welled up along cracks; the eruption of the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province coincided with the end-Triassic mass extinction. First the Atlantic opened between North America and Africa, then Gondwana split into South America, Africa, Antarctica, Australia and India. India drifted north at up to 15 cm a year and collided with Asia about 50 million years ago, raising the Himalaya. The separation of continents explains why marsupials dominate Australia and why fossils of the same reptiles appear in India, Africa and Antarctica.

name: Chicxulub asteroid impact
impact: ~75% of species lost, incl. non-avian dinosaurs
summary: A ~10 km asteroid hit Yucatán; mammals later inherited the Earth.
details: About 66 million years ago an asteroid roughly 10 km wide struck the Yucatán Peninsula, gouging a crater 180 km across and releasing energy equal to billions of atomic bombs. Tsunamis, global wildfires and a 'impact winter' of soot and sulphate aerosols blocked sunlight for years, collapsing food chains. About three-quarters of all species died, including all non-bird dinosaurs; the iridium-rich clay layer found worldwide (identified by Luis and Walter Alvarez in 1980) is its fingerprint. India's Deccan Traps eruptions at the same time added climate stress. Small mammals survived and later diversified, eventually leading to primates and humans.

name: Onset of the Quaternary ice ages
summary: Ice sheets advanced and retreated about every 41,000, then 100,000 years.
details: Around 2.6 million years ago, Earth's climate cooled enough for great ice sheets to grow and shrink over the northern continents in cycles paced by variations in Earth's orbit (Milankovitch cycles), at first every 41,000 years and, after about 1 million years ago, every 100,000 years. Africa became drier and more variable, with savannas expanding — a backdrop to the emergence of the genus Homo and stone tool making. Falling sea levels repeatedly exposed land bridges such as Beringia and Sundaland, which humans later crossed.

name: Toba super-eruption
impact: Ash layer across India; debated effect on humans
summary: One of the largest eruptions in 2 million years; Indian sites like Jwalapuram suggest people survived it.
details: The Youngest Toba eruption in Sumatra about 74,000 years ago ejected roughly 2,800 cubic km of material, leaving Lake Toba's caldera and spreading ash over India, where a layer up to several metres thick still lies. Scientists once argued it caused a 'volcanic winter' and a human population bottleneck. Excavations at Jwalapuram in Andhra Pradesh found stone tools above and below the ash, and studies in South Africa suggest people coped, so its human impact is now debated rather than assumed catastrophic.

name: Last Glacial Maximum
impact: Sea level ~120 m lower; land bridges
summary: Humans crossed Beringia into the Americas around this time or after.
details: Between about 26,000 and 19,000 years ago ice sheets reached their greatest recent extent, covering Canada, Scandinavia and the British Isles under up to 3 km of ice. Sea level was about 120 m lower, joining Britain to Europe, Sri Lanka to India and Siberia to Alaska. People retreated to refugia such as southern France, Iberia and Ukraine, hunting mammoth and reindeer and building mammoth-bone huts. As the ice melted, they recolonised northern lands and the Americas were settled.

name: Younger Dryas
summary: A sudden 1,200-year chill, possibly from meltwater shutting the Atlantic circulation.
details: About 12,900 years ago, while the world was warming, the Northern Hemisphere abruptly snapped back to near-glacial cold for about 1,200 years, probably because meltwater weakened the Atlantic's ocean currents. In the Levant the cold and drought may have pushed Natufian foragers to cultivate wild cereals, a step toward farming. It ended suddenly around 11,700 years ago, marking the start of the Holocene, the warm, stable climate in which agriculture and civilisation developed.

name: Quaternary megafauna extinction
impact: Mammoths, giant sloths, cave lions vanish
summary: Caused by human hunting combined with climate change.
details: Between about 50,000 and 10,000 years ago, most large animals over 45 kg disappeared from Australia, the Americas and northern Eurasia: mammoths, mastodons, giant ground sloths, Diprotodon, Smilodon and many others. The timing often follows human arrival — Australia around 45,000 years ago, the Americas around 13,000 years ago — suggesting hunting played a big part, combined with climate change at the end of the Ice Age. Africa and South Asia, where animals evolved alongside humans, lost far fewer species.

name: End of the Green Sahara
summary: Drying pushed people into the Nile valley as Egypt's state formed.
details: During the African Humid Period (about 14,500–5,500 years ago), stronger monsoon rains turned the Sahara into grassland with lakes, hippos and crocodiles; rock art shows cattle herders and swimmers. As Earth's orbit shifted, rains weakened and the Sahara dried, sometimes abruptly, around 5,500 years ago. Herders moved toward the Nile and the Sahel, a migration that some historians link to the concentration of people that led to Egyptian civilisation.

name: 4.2-kiloyear drought
impact: Collapse of Akkad, Egypt's Old Kingdom; Indus decline
summary: Defines the start of the Meghalayan Age, named from a Meghalaya cave stalagmite.
details: Around 2200 BCE a severe, centuries-long drought affected regions from the Mediterranean to India and China. It coincides with the collapse of the Akkadian Empire, the end of Egypt's Old Kingdom, and changes in the Indus Valley, where cities later declined as monsoons weakened. It is used to define the boundary between the Middle and Late Holocene (the Meghalayan Age, named after a cave in Meghalaya, India).

name: Thera (Santorini) eruption
summary: One of the largest eruptions of human history.
details: Around 1600 BCE the volcanic island of Thera exploded in one of the largest eruptions of the past 10,000 years. It buried the Minoan town of Akrotiri under ash (its inhabitants had already fled), triggered tsunamis on Crete, and probably weakened Minoan civilisation. Some scholars think it inspired the legend of Atlantis.

name: Eruption of Vesuvius
summary: Preserved a Roman town frozen in time.
details: On 24–25 August 79 CE (some evidence suggests October), Vesuvius buried Pompeii and Herculaneum under ash and pyroclastic flows, killing perhaps 2,000 people. Pliny the Younger described the eruption in letters; his uncle Pliny the Elder died trying to rescue people. Preserved houses, bread and graffiti make Pompeii a snapshot of everyday Roman life.

name: Volcanic winter of 536
impact: 'The worst year to be alive'; crop failures
summary: Followed by the Late Antique Little Ice Age and Justinian's plague.
details: In 536 CE an eruption, probably in Iceland, filled the Northern Hemisphere sky with dust; Procopius wrote that the sun shone without brightness for a year. Summer temperatures fell sharply, crops failed from Ireland to China, and further eruptions in 539–540 deepened the cold of the Late Antique Little Ice Age. It was followed by the Plague of Justinian.

name: Tambora eruption
summary: Caused famine in Europe; possibly linked to a new cholera strain in Bengal (1817).
details: Mount Tambora on Sumbawa, Indonesia, erupted in April 1815, the largest eruption in recorded history, killing over 70,000 people locally. Its aerosols caused 1816's 'Year Without a Summer', with crop failures in Europe and North America, and contributed to a cholera outbreak in Bengal. That cold summer, Mary Shelley wrote Frankenstein.

name: Krakatoa eruption
summary: Its sound was heard 4,800 km away.
details: After months of activity, Krakatoa, a volcanic island between Java and Sumatra, exploded on 27 August 1883 with a blast heard 4,800 km away on Rodrigues Island — the loudest sound in recorded history. Tsunamis up to 40 m high killed about 36,000 people on nearby coasts. Ash cooled global temperatures by about 1.2 °C and caused blood-red sunsets for months; telegraph cables spread the news worldwide within hours. A new island, Anak Krakatau ('child of Krakatoa'), emerged in 1927.

name: Plague of Athens
impact: Killed perhaps a quarter of Athens, including Pericles
summary: Struck during the Peloponnesian War.
details: In 430 BCE, in the second year of the Peloponnesian War, an epidemic struck Athens, crowded with refugees inside the Long Walls. It killed perhaps a quarter of the population, including the leader Pericles. Thucydides, who survived it, described its symptoms; its cause is still debated (typhoid is one candidate).

name: Antonine Plague
summary: Brought back by soldiers from Mesopotamia.
details: Roman troops returning from the siege of Seleucia in Mesopotamia brought an epidemic around 165 CE, probably smallpox, which spread across the empire. The physician Galen described fever, diarrhoea and a black rash. It may have killed 10% of the population — 5 to 10 million people — including perhaps co-emperor Lucius Verus, and it recurred in 189 CE. Labour and army shortages weakened Marcus Aurelius's defence of the Danube frontier.

summary: The first plague pandemic.
details: From 541 CE the bubonic plague (Yersinia pestis, confirmed by ancient DNA) spread from Egypt across the Byzantine Empire; Constantinople may have lost thousands a day at its peak. Recurrences for two centuries weakened Byzantium and Persia just before the Arab conquests.

name: Black Death
summary: Spread along Mongol trade routes; transformed labour and religion.
details: Yersinia pestis, carried by fleas on rats and spread along trade routes from Central Asia, reached the Crimea in 1346 and Europe in 1347. Within five years it killed perhaps a third to half of Europe's population and many in the Middle East. Labour shortages raised wages, weakened serfdom and fuelled revolts, while persecutions of Jews followed. Repeated outbreaks continued until the 18th century.

name: Smallpox in the Americas
impact: Up to ~90% of Indigenous people died
summary: Smallpox, measles and flu brought by Europeans.
details: Europeans brought smallpox, measles and influenza, to which Native Americans had no immunity. Smallpox reached Mexico in 1520 and devastated Tenochtitlan during Cortés's siege, and swept through the Inca Empire, killing the emperor Huayna Capac and triggering civil war. Epidemics may have killed up to 90% of the indigenous population over a century.

name: Cholera pandemics
summary: The first pandemic began in the Ganges delta; John Snow traced cholera to water in 1854.
details: Cholera, a waterborne bacterial disease, had long been endemic in the Ganges delta. In 1817 it spread along British military and trade routes to Asia, the Middle East and Russia, then to Europe and the Americas in later waves; seven pandemics have occurred, the latest beginning in 1961. In 1854 John Snow traced a London outbreak to a contaminated water pump, and Robert Koch identified the bacterium in Calcutta in 1884. These discoveries led cities to build sewers and clean water supplies.

summary: Bombay's 1896 plague led to harsh British measures; Yersin found the bacterium.
details: Beginning in Yunnan, China in the 1850s, bubonic plague reached Hong Kong in 1894 and Bombay in 1896 via shipping. India suffered about 12 million deaths of the global 15 million. name: Spanish flu
summary: India suffered the most deaths of any country.
details: A deadly H1N1 influenza strain spread in three waves from 1918 to 1920, carried by troopships at the end of World War I. It infected about a third of the world's population and killed perhaps 50 million, unusually striking healthy young adults. India lost an estimated 12–17 million, more than any other country, as the virus arrived via Bombay with returning soldiers during a drought. It was called 'Spanish' only because neutral Spain's newspapers reported it freely.

name: HIV/AIDS pandemic
summary: Antiretroviral drugs turned it into a manageable condition.
details: HIV-1 crossed from chimpanzees to humans in southeastern Cameroon, probably through bushmeat hunting, and spread via colonial-era Kinshasa in the early 20th century. AIDS was recognised in 1981 and HIV identified in 1983. About 40 million people have died, and sub-Saharan Africa was hit hardest. Antiretroviral therapy since 1996, and later cheaper Indian generic drugs, turned it into a manageable chronic condition.

name: COVID-19 pandemic
summary: Led to lockdowns and record-speed vaccines.
details: A new coronavirus, SARS-CoV-2, was identified in Wuhan, China, in December 2019 and declared a pandemic on 11 March 2020. Lockdowns closed schools and borders worldwide; India's 2021 Delta wave overwhelmed hospitals and oxygen supplies. mRNA and other vaccines were developed within a year, and India produced Covishield and Covaxin. WHO estimates over 7 million recorded deaths, with excess deaths perhaps closer to 15–20 million.

name: Invention of writing
summary: Cuneiform and hieroglyphs started as accounting marks.
details: Writing was invented independently at least four times: in Mesopotamia (cuneiform, about 3200 BCE), Egypt (hieroglyphs, about 3200 BCE), China (oracle bones, about 1250 BCE) and Mesoamerica (about 900–600 BCE). In Sumer it grew from clay tokens used for accounting to record goods, then laws, letters and literature. Writing let states keep records, collect taxes and preserve knowledge across generations — the dividing line between prehistory and history.

name: Buddha's enlightenment
summary: Siddhartha Gautama became the Buddha under the Bodhi tree.
details: Prince Siddhartha Gautama of the Shakya clan, born at Lumbini, renounced his comfortable life after seeing old age, sickness and death. After six years of extreme austerity, he chose a 'middle way' and meditated under a pipal tree at Bodh Gaya until he attained enlightenment, becoming the Buddha ('awakened one'), probably in the 5th century BCE. He gave his first sermon at Sarnath on the Four Noble Truths, and taught for 45 years across the Ganga plain.

Victory gave Athens confidence and an empire, leading to its golden age.

name: Kalinga War
summary: Led Ashoka to spread Buddhism and dhamma.
details: Kalinga, on India's east coast, controlled sea trade to Southeast Asia and had resisted Mauryan rule. About 261 BCE Ashoka conquered it. His own Rock Edict XIII records that 150,000 people were deported, 100,000 killed and many more died of famine and disease. Ashoka's remorse turned him toward Buddhism and dhamma; he gave up wars of conquest in favour of 'conquest by righteousness'.

name: Unification of China under Qin
summary: Standardised writing, coins and weights.
details: Between 230 and 221 BCE, King Ying Zheng of Qin, using Legalist reforms that made Qin's farmers and soldiers efficient and disciplined, conquered the six other Warring States one by one: Han, Zhao, Wei, Chu, Yan and Qi. He proclaimed himself Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor. He standardised writing, coins, laws and axle widths and created commanderies run by appointed officials, which shaped Chinese government for two millennia.

name: Punic Wars
summary: Hannibal crossed the Alps with elephants.
details: Rome and Carthage fought three wars over the western Mediterranean. In the First (264–241 BCE) Rome built a navy and won Sicily; in the Second (218–201 BCE) Hannibal crossed the Alps with elephants and destroyed Roman armies at Lake Trasimene and Cannae, but Scipio invaded Africa and defeated him at Zama. In the Third (149–146 BCE) Rome besieged and destroyed Carthage, selling its survivors into slavery.

name: Roman conquest of Gaul
summary: Julius Caesar defeated Vercingetorix at Alesia.
details: Julius Caesar, governor of Gaul from 58 BCE, used conflicts among Gallic tribes to intervene, defeating the Helvetii, Belgae and Veneti and crossing to Britain and the Rhine. In 52 BCE the Arverni chief Vercingetorix united the Gauls; Caesar besieged him at Alesia and defeated a relief army. Plutarch claims a million Gauls died and a million were enslaved. Gaul became Romanised, and French developed from Latin.

details: Emperor Claudius invaded in 43 CE with four legions, seeking glory. name: Assassination of Julius Caesar
summary: Led to Augustus becoming emperor.
details: After winning the civil war, Caesar was named dictator for life in 44 BCE, alarming senators who feared monarchy. On the Ides of March, about 60 conspirators led by Brutus and Cassius stabbed him 23 times at a Senate meeting in the Theatre of Pompey. Instead of restoring the Republic, his death led to civil wars between the conspirators and Antony and Octavian, ending in Augustus's empire.

name: Crucifixion of Jesus
summary: Christianity became Rome's state religion by 380.
details: Jesus, a Jewish preacher from Galilee, came to Jerusalem at Passover around 30–33 CE. Temple authorities saw him as a threat, and the Roman prefect Pontius Pilate had him crucified, a punishment for rebels. His followers proclaimed that he rose from the dead; the apostle Paul and others spread the faith across the Roman world, and Christianity became the empire's religion by the late 4th century.

name: Hijra and rise of Islam
summary: Prophet Muhammad moved from Mecca to Medina.
details: Muhammad began preaching in Mecca around 610, facing persecution from the Quraysh elite. In 622 he and his followers migrated to Yathrib (Medina), where he led a community governed by the Constitution of Medina — the year 1 of the Islamic calendar. After battles at Badr, Uhud and the Trench, Mecca surrendered in 630, and by his death in 632 most of Arabia had accepted Islam.

name: Arab conquest of Sindh
impact: Islam arrives in South Asia by land
summary: Led by Muhammad bin Qasim.
details: After pirates seized ships carrying gifts to the Umayyad governor al-Hajjaj, he sent his 17-year-old nephew Muhammad bin Qasim to Sindh. Sindh became an Umayyad province, Hindus and Buddhists were treated as protected people paying jizya, and Arab scholars learned Indian mathematics and astronomy.

summary: Charles Martel's victory.
details: After conquering Spain from 711, Umayyad armies raided into Gaul. name: Battle of Hastings
summary: William the Conqueror defeated Harold II.
details: Edward the Confessor died childless in January 1066, and three men claimed England's throne. Harold Godwinson was crowned, defeated the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada at Stamford Bridge, then marched south to meet William of Normandy, who had landed at Pevensey. On 14 October 1066, after a day-long fight, Harold was killed (perhaps by an arrow in the eye, as the Bayeux Tapestry suggests). William was crowned on Christmas Day, built castles, replaced the English nobility with Normans and ordered the Domesday Book; French words flooded into English.

name: First Crusade
summary: The start of two centuries of crusades.
details: In 1095, after the Byzantine emperor asked for help against the Seljuk Turks, Pope Urban II called on Western Christians to free Jerusalem, promising remission of sins. A popular 'People's Crusade' massacred Jews in the Rhineland before being destroyed in Anatolia. The knights' armies took Antioch (1098) and Jerusalem (July 1099), slaughtering many Muslim and Jewish inhabitants, and founded four crusader states. Muslim memory of this violence shaped later relations, and Saladin retook Jerusalem in 1187.

name: Second Battle of Tarain
impact: Muhammad of Ghor defeats Prithviraj Chauhan
summary: Opened North India to the Delhi Sultanate.
details: In 1191 the Chauhan king Prithviraj III defeated Muhammad of Ghor at Tarain near Thanesar. Ghori returned in 1192 with mounted archers who used feigned retreats to break the Rajput army; Prithviraj was captured and killed. Ghori's slave-general Qutb ud-Din Aibak took Delhi, and after Ghori's death founded the Delhi Sultanate in 1206, beginning six centuries of Turkic, Afghan and Mughal rule in north India.

name: Mongol conquests
summary: The largest contiguous land empire.
details: After Temüjin was proclaimed Genghis Khan in 1206, Mongol armies of mounted archers, organised in decimal units with strict discipline and fast messengers, conquered northern China, destroyed the Khwarazmian Empire (1219–21), and, under his successors, Russia (1237–40), Baghdad (1258) and all of China (1279). Cities that resisted were often massacred; tens of millions may have died. Yet the Pax Mongolica also reopened the Silk Road, allowing Marco Polo's travels and the spread of gunpowder, paper and, tragically, the Black Death. They were stopped by the Mamluks at Ain Jalut (1260), the Delhi Sultanate, and storms off Japan.

name: Destruction of Nalanda
summary: Attributed to Bakhtiyar Khilji's forces.
details: Nalanda, a great monastic university founded in the 5th century, had trained scholars from China, Tibet and Korea for 700 years. Around 1193 forces of Bakhtiyar Khalji sacked Nalanda and Vikramashila, killing monks; the Persian historian Minhaj-i-Siraj records the attacks, and later tradition says the library burned for months. Combined with the decline of royal patronage, it ended institutional Buddhism in India, though it survived in Tibet, Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia. A new Nalanda University opened nearby in 2014.

name: Magna Carta
summary: An early step toward constitutional rule.
details: King John of England lost Normandy to France, raised heavy taxes and quarrelled with the Pope. In June 1215 rebel barons forced him to seal the 'Great Charter' at Runnymede, which said that no free man could be imprisoned or punished except by lawful judgement of his peers or the law of the land, and that the king must consult barons on taxes. The Pope annulled it within weeks and civil war followed, but reissued versions became part of English law. Later, Parliament, American colonists and Indian freedom fighters cited it as a symbol of rights against arbitrary power.

name: Sack of Baghdad
impact: End of the Abbasid Caliphate; House of Wisdom destroyed
summary: By Hulagu Khan.
details: Hulagu Khan's Mongol army, with Christian Georgian and Armenian allies and Chinese siege engineers, besieged Baghdad in January–February 1258. After the caliph al-Musta'sim surrendered, the city was sacked for a week; estimates of the dead range from tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands, and the caliph was reportedly rolled in a carpet and trampled. The House of Wisdom's books were said to have turned the Tigris black with ink. The fall ended the Abbasid caliphate in Baghdad and shifted Islamic cultural centres to Cairo, Delhi and later Istanbul.

name: Fall of Constantinople
summary: Ottoman cannons broke the walls.
details: By 1453 the Byzantine Empire was little more than its capital, defended by about 7,000 men. Sultan Mehmed II, 21 years old, besieged it with perhaps 80,000 troops and giant bronze cannon cast by the Hungarian engineer Orban, and dragged ships overland into the Golden Horn. On 29 May the walls were breached; the last emperor, Constantine XI, died fighting. Mehmed made the city his capital, turned Hagia Sophia into a mosque, and Greek scholars who fled to Italy helped fuel the Renaissance; Europeans sought sea routes to Asia, leading to the Age of Exploration.

name: Gutenberg printing press
summary: Movable type printing in Europe.
details: Around 1440–1450 in Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg combined movable metal type cast in a hand mould, oil-based ink and a screw press adapted from wine presses. His Bible (about 1455) was printed in some 180 copies. By 1500 presses in over 250 European cities had printed perhaps 20 million volumes. Printing spread Renaissance learning, made Luther's Reformation possible and standardised languages. Earlier, China had invented woodblock printing (Diamond Sutra, 868) and Korea metal type (Jikji, 1377).

name: Columbus reaches the Americas
summary: Connected the Old and New Worlds.
details: Christopher Columbus, a Genoese navigator sponsored by Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain, sailed west seeking Asia and landed in the Bahamas on 12 October 1492, then reached Cuba and Hispaniola. He believed he had reached the Indies, hence the name 'Indians'. His voyages began European colonisation, the Columbian Exchange of crops and animals, the enslavement and catastrophic population collapse of the Taíno and other peoples, and later the Atlantic slave trade.

impact: Sea route from Europe to India
summary: Began European colonial trade in Asia.
details: Sailing around the Cape of Good Hope with an East African pilot's help, Vasco da Gama reached Calicut (Kozhikode) on 20 May 1498. Portugal soon used warships and forts (Goa, 1510) to control Indian Ocean trade, beginning European colonial involvement in India.

name: First Battle of Panipat
summary: Babur's cannons defeated Ibrahim Lodi.
details: On 21 April 1526 Babur, ruler of Kabul, with about 12,000–25,000 men, met Sultan Ibrahim Lodi's much larger army and about 100 elephants. Babur used the tulughma flanking tactic and field guns and matchlocks behind carts; the guns panicked the elephants. Ibrahim Lodi died in battle, the first Indian ruler killed on the battlefield in this era, and Babur founded the Mughal Empire.

name: Fall of Tenochtitlan

details: Hernán Cortés landed in Mexico in 1519 with about 500 men and allied with the Tlaxcalans and others who resented Aztec tribute. After a 75-day siege with brigantines on the lake, Tenochtitlan fell on 13 August 1521; Mexico City was built on its ruins.

impact: A trading company that conquered India
summary: Granted a royal charter by Elizabeth I.
details: On 31 December 1600 Elizabeth I chartered the 'Governor and Company of Merchants of London trading into the East Indies'. name: Atlantic slave trade
summary: One of history's greatest crimes.
details: From the 16th to 19th centuries about 12.5 million Africans were shipped across the Atlantic, and nearly 2 million died on the Middle Passage. Enslaved people worked on sugar, tobacco and cotton plantations in Brazil, the Caribbean and North America. African resistance, revolts like Haiti's, and abolitionist movements led Britain to ban the trade in 1807 and slavery in 1833; Brazil was last in 1888.

details: On 23 June 1757 Robert Clive's 3,000 troops faced Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah's 50,000. Clive had bribed the Nawab's commander Mir Jafar, who held back his troops. The Nawab fled and was killed; Mir Jafar became a puppet Nawab, and the Company gained control of Bengal's revenues.

name: Third Battle of Panipat
impact: Marathas defeated by Ahmad Shah Durrani
summary: One of the bloodiest battles of the 18th century.
details: The Marathas, controlling much of India, clashed with Afghan ruler Ahmad Shah Durrani, allied with Najib-ud-Daula and Shuja-ud-Daula. After months of standoff, the hungry Maratha army under Sadashivrao Bhau attacked on 14 January 1761 and was annihilated; Vishwasrao and Bhau died. Perhaps 100,000 died including civilians. It halted Maratha expansion and left a power vacuum the British exploited.

name: Great Bengal Famine
impact: ~10 million dead (about a third of Bengal)
summary: Worsened by Company revenue collection.
details: In 1769–70 a failed monsoon struck Bengal and Bihar. The Company, newly in charge of revenue, kept collecting taxes and its officials hoarded rice. About 10 million people — a third of Bengal's population — died, and farmland went back to jungle. It is a classic example of colonial famine policy.

name: American Revolution
summary: Inspired later anti-colonial movements.
details: After the Seven Years' War, Britain taxed its American colonies (Stamp Act, Tea Act), provoking protests like the Boston Tea Party (1773). Fighting began at Lexington and Concord in 1775; the Declaration of Independence (4 July 1776), written by Thomas Jefferson, declared that 'all men are created equal'. With French help, George Washington won at Yorktown (1781), and the US Constitution (1787) created a federal republic.

name: French Revolution
impact: End of absolute monarchy; 'Liberty, equality, fraternity'

details: France was bankrupt from wars, and bread prices were high. In 1789 the Third Estate formed a National Assembly, crowds stormed the Bastille, and feudal privileges were abolished. Napoleon seized power in 1799, but the ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity spread worldwide.

name: Haitian Revolution
impact: First nation founded by formerly enslaved people
summary: Led by Toussaint Louverture.
details: Saint-Domingue was the world's richest colony, producing sugar with about 500,000 enslaved Africans. Napoleon tried to restore slavery and captured Toussaint, but Jean-Jacques Dessalines defeated the French, and Haiti declared independence on 1 January 1804.

name: Napoleonic Wars

details: Napoleon, crowned emperor in 1804, won brilliant victories at Austerlitz (1805), Jena (1806) and Wagram (1809), dominating Europe and spreading the Napoleonic Code. name: Opium Wars
summary: Britain forced China to accept opium grown in India.
details: British merchants smuggled opium grown in Bengal into China to pay for tea, creating millions of addicts. When Commissioner Lin Zexu destroyed 1,400 tonnes of opium at Canton in 1839, Britain sent gunboats; the Treaty of Nanking (1842) ceded Hong Kong, opened five ports and imposed an indemnity. A Second Opium War (1856–60) with France ended with the looting and burning of the Old Summer Palace and legalised opium. China calls the era that followed the 'century of humiliation'.

name: Abolition of slavery in the British Empire
summary: Indentured Indian labourers then went to Mauritius, Fiji, the Caribbean.
details: Campaigners such as Olaudah Equiano, Thomas Clarkson and William Wilberforce, along with major slave revolts in Jamaica (Baptist War, 1831–32), pushed Parliament to end the slave trade (1807) and then slavery itself. The Slavery Abolition Act of 1833 freed about 800,000 people from 1834, though most had to serve 'apprenticeships' until 1838. Slave owners received £20 million in compensation — the enslaved received nothing. Plantation owners then turned to indentured labourers from India, sending over a million to the Caribbean, Mauritius, Fiji and Africa.

name: American Civil War
summary: Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation.
details: When Abraham Lincoln was elected in 1860 on a platform opposing slavery's expansion, eleven southern states seceded as the Confederacy. Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation (1863) and the 13th Amendment (1865) abolished slavery; Lincoln was assassinated days after the Confederacy surrendered at Appomattox.

name: Scramble for Africa
summary: The Berlin Conference divided the continent.
details: In 1870 Europeans controlled about 10% of Africa; by 1914 only Ethiopia and Liberia remained independent. Quinine, steamships and the Maxim gun gave Europeans an edge. Borders drawn at the Berlin Conference (1884–85) ignored ethnic and linguistic realities. Colonial rule brought forced labour, the Congo atrocities, the Herero and Nama genocide in German South-West Africa, and economies built around exporting raw materials.

summary: El Niño drought plus colonial grain policy.
details: A failed monsoon linked to a strong El Niño hit Madras, Mysore, Hyderabad and Bombay presidencies. Viceroy Lytton, following free-market principles, refused to control prices while grain was exported to Britain, and relief camps gave rations (the 'Temple wage') below those in Buchenwald, as historian Mike Davis notes. Some 5.5–10 million people died. Outrage over this famine helped give birth to Indian economic nationalism and the Congress.

summary: Early leaders included Dadabhai Naoroji.

name: World War I
summary: About 1.3 million Indian soldiers served.
details: Rivalries, an arms race and alliances turned the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo (28 June 1914) into a world war. The war destroyed the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman empires and set the stage for World War II.

Tagore renounced his knighthood, and Udham Singh later shot Michael O'Dwyer, Punjab's former governor, in London (1940).

name: Indian Independence and Partition
impact: India and Pakistan created; ~15 million displaced, up to ~2 million killed

details: In 1991 India's foreign reserves could cover only weeks of imports, and it pledged gold to borrow. Prime Minister P. V. name: First upright walking

name: Neanderthal extinction

details: Sati, the burning of widows on their husband's pyre, was practised among some communities, with hundreds of cases a year recorded in Bengal. Raja Ram Mohan Roy campaigned against it, quoting scriptures. In 1829 Governor-General Bentinck's Regulation XVII made sati illegal, and the Privy Council rejected an appeal by orthodox groups in 1832.

details: In February 1835 Thomas Babington Macaulay argued that government money should fund English education rather than Sanskrit and Arabic, claiming 'a single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole native literature of India'. Bentinck adopted it in the English Education Act. It created an English-educated middle class that later led the freedom movement.

details: Potato blight (Phytophthora infestans) struck in 1845, destroying the staple food of Ireland's poor. British relief was limited and food exports continued. details: Economic crisis and demands for constitutions and national unity sparked revolts in France, the German and Italian states, Austria and Hungary in 1848. Most revolts were crushed by 1849, but serfdom was abolished in Austria, and that year Marx and Engels published The Communist Manifesto.

name: Meiji Restoration
summary: End of the shogunate.
details: After Commodore Perry forced Japan open (1853–54), samurai from Satsuma and Chōshū rebelled against the Tokugawa shogunate and restored power to the young Emperor Meiji in 1868. Japan defeated China (1895) and Russia (1905).
